subject: Civil Engineering
title: Columns: Standing Under Pressure
description: A micro-lesson that makes Columns: Standing Under Pressure usable.

hook.text: The Parthenon has stood on marble columns for 2,500 years. Compression keeps them up.

buildup.text: Columns carry vertical loads straight down. Short columns crush; long columns buckle.

discovery.text: Euler's formula predicts when a slender column will buckle based on length and stiffness.

twist.text: A column twice as long buckles at one-quarter the load — length matters enormously.

climax.text: Engineers add bracing or make columns wider to prevent sudden buckling collapse.

punchline.text: Columns don't crush — they buckle sideways and fold.

quiz.question: What happens when you double the length of a slender column?
options: Its buckling load drops to one quarter
Its buckling load stays the same

details.summary: Columns are vertical compression members that transfer loads from beams and floors down to the foundation. Short columns fail by material crushing when stress exceeds compressive strength.
details.whyItMatters: Columns carry the accumulated weight of every floor above them. Column failure is catastrophic because it can trigger progressive collapse of the entire structure above the failed column.
takeaways: Short stocky columns fail by material crushing at the compressive strength limit
Long slender columns fail by buckling at loads well below material strength
Euler's formula predicts the critical buckling load based on length and stiffness

faq.question: What determines whether a column fails by crushing or buckling?
faq.answer: The slenderness ratio, which is the effective length divided by the radius of gyration of the cross-section, determines failure mode. Below a critical slenderness ratio (roughly 60 to 100 depending on material), the column crushes. Above it, the column buckles elastically.

faq.question: How does Euler's buckling formula work?
faq.answer: Euler's critical load equals pi squared times the elastic modulus times the moment of inertia, divided by the square of the effective length. Doubling the length reduces the buckling load to one quarter.
